title: Kernel Fusion Boundary Investigation
content:
Purpose:
This scratchpad captures an exploratory investigation into the practical boundary where kernel fusion stops improving end-to-end latency and starts regressing due to shape variability, memory fragmentation, and scheduling interference. Our goal is simple: identify the regimes (batch size, seq len distribution, kv cache hit rate, and fused-op mix) where fused attention+matmul kernels are net-positive, and where falling back to piecemeal FlashAttention or paged attention is better for 95th/99th percentile latency and p50 cost/token.

Background / Motivation:
- We ship a fused-ops execution path that combines QK matmul, scaled softmax, dropout (when enabled), and final matmul in one fused kernel on our CUDA backend. This reduces global memory traffic for stable shapes.
- FlashAttention-style kernels (memory-friendly attention) excel on wide single-shot sequences but depend on contiguous attention loops; paged attention (our allocator-backed split across KV pages) helps very long contexts.
- Anecdotal SRE alerts over the last two months show tail latency spikes for small bursty traffic (batches of 1-4 with sequence lengths 64->512 mixed) after we enabled fusion heuristics by default.

Hypothesis:
1) Fusion helps when most elements in a micro-batch share a narrow seq-len bucket (low variance).
2) Fusion regresses when: (a) shape variance causes warp underutilization, (b) alignment to scratchpad/SM memory causes additional periods of kernel-level serialization, or (c) paged-KV transfers overlap badly with the fused kernel's large shared-memory footprint.

Key metrics to collect (ordered by priority):
- p50/p95/p99 end-to-end request latency (ms)
- kernel-level latency distribution (ms) per CUDA stream
- SM occupancy and registers/spill (NVIDIA SMI / Nsight counters)
- L2 read/write and global DRAM bandwidth utilization
- Warp-level execution efficiency / divergence
- Page fault / pager transfer bytes (for paged attention)
- CPU scheduling spikes and stream queue lengths

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Batch sizes: 1, 2, 4, 8
- Sequence lengths: uniform (64/128/256/512) and mixed (random uniform between 16-512, 8 samples per request)
- KV cache hit ratios: 0% (cold), 50% (partial), 100% (hot) — emulate by preloading KV for a subset of requests
- Model widths: 2048, 4096 hidden size equivalent (to exercise different matmul sizes)
- Fusion toggles: Full fusion (default), Partial fusion (no dropout fused), No fusion (FlashAttention-only), Paged-attention fallback enabled/disabled

Microbench commands (local test rig):
- baseline flashattention run: ./bench_runner --model gpt-medium --seq 256 --batch 4 --mode flash --reps 200 --profile
- fused kernel run: ./bench_runner --model gpt-medium --seq 256 --batch 4 --mode fused --fuse_dropout=1 --reps 200 --profile
- mixed shapes: python tools/run_mixed_shapes.py --shapes 16,64,128,512 --batch 4 --mode fused,flash --reps 300
- pager stress: ./pager_torture --seq-len 4096 --page-size 1024 --kv-hot-ratio 0.3 --run-time 180

What to capture per run:
1. stdout timeline with per-request latencies (raw)
2. nvprof/Nsight logs for each run (kernel names, durations, occupancy)
3. top-level process perf/psutil CPU wakeups + device queues at 10ms granularity
4. a simple histogram dump of shape distribution seen in the run (so we can correlate shapes -> kernel choices)

Preliminary observations (short runs on ci-inference-03):
- With batch=1 and mixed shapes, full fusion increases p95 by ~12-18% vs FlashAttention-only, while p50 is ~5% better. This implies fusion reduces average latency (improved per-token cost) but increases the tail due to serialization on the GPU for malformed shapes.
- For batch=8 and uniform seq=512, fusion wins across p50/p95/p99 by 20-30% — expected due to high throughput and good occupancy.
- When paged-KV transfers are concurrently active, fused kernels sometimes stall waiting on L2/DRAM (Nsight shows heavy L2 eviction churn). The fused kernel's scratchpad pressure seems to amplify paging overheads.

Notable kernel traces (human notes):
- Kernel name: fused_attn_qk_softmax_mm_fwd — when shape variance high, multiple launches with small grid sizes appear sequentially instead of one large launch (scheduler fragmentation).
- Kernel name: flash_attn_fwd — consistent launch grid sizes, lower shared memory use, but higher global DRAM reads because of intermediate writes.

Open questions to validate next runs:
- Is the tail coming from serialization on the GPU (kernel launches queued on same stream because the fused kernel occasionally sets cudaDeviceSynchronize internally for correctness with our allocator)? Check callers for implicit syncs.
- Does reducing fused kernel shared-memory footprint (drop per-thread tile buffer) recover tails? We should compile a variant with reduced tile size and test.
- Can we use a hybrid runtime heuristic: prefer fusion for seq_len >= X and batch >= Y and seq_variance < Z? If so, we need a cheap estimator of seq_variance at enqueue time.

Quick-win hypotheses to test (ordered):
1) Enforce per-stream concurrency: try running fused kernel on a dedicated CUDA stream per request to reduce serialization (cost: more streams to manage).
2) Introduce a cheap shape-hash probe before fusion: sample first token or first 8 tokens to estimate sequence length cohorts; fallback to FlashAttention if high variance in micro-batch.
3) Reduce scratchpad allocation to a conservative mode under high pager load.

Experiment schedule (near term):
- Sprint week 1: implement shape-cohort estimator and a runtime flag to bypass fusion when cohort skew > threshold. Lightweight, low-risk. Owner: Ethan.
- Sprint week 2: compile reduced-tile fused kernel variant and run shape-sweep matrix for batch 1..8 x seq 32..1024. Owner: Lina.
- Sprint week 3: pager overlap runs on real traffic replay (24-hour) with toggles for fused/no-fused, evaluate p99. Owner: Priya + SRE pairing.

Data collection template (CSV columns):
run_id, run_mode, batch_size, seq_dist, kv_hot_ratio, model_width, p50, p95, p99, avg_kernel_sm_occupancy, l2_bytes, global_bytes, warp_efficiency, notes

Quick notes to self:
- When creating replay traces, ensure we include the same stream submission pattern as prod (we used a single submit thread in past tests, which skews timings).
- Add a microbench that randomizes stream assignment to simulate multi-request concurrency.
- Remember to bump perf CI timeout for batch 8 seq 1024 runs (they take longer).

Risks / Danger signs:
- If fusion toggles lead to flaky correctness under path-dependent race conditions, revert. Always run diff-based output checks (logprob match within epsilon) after kernel change.
- Pager stress tests on shared infra can cause noisy neighbors; prefer dedicated node for these runs.

Appendix: small checklist before next run:
- [ ] Land instrumentation PR that logs per-request chosen kernel (PR: #842 linked above)
- [ ] Add shape variance telemetry to runtime trace messages (lightweight histogram per second)
- [ ] Build reduced-tile fused kernel variant (label: fused-conservative-tile)

Slack refs / threads:
- #serving-runtime: "fusion-default-rollout" (thread ts 17123345) — people reported p99 spikes
- #sre-ops: "nvlink-pager-bumping" — correlated time window 2024-06-27 02:00Z

Conclusion (working):
Fusion is still a net win for throughput-heavy, shape-stable workloads. For our mixed, bursty, low-batch production traffic we need a simple runtime heuristic to avoid fusion for high-shape-variance micro-batches or when pager activity is elevated. Next steps are to (1) collect more controlled replay data against a shape-sweep grid, (2) land a shape-cohort probe and run A/B experiments in staging, and (3) measure cost/throughput delta to determine flip threshold for production rollout.
